directed.conceptual_reading: The H^{1/2} norm identifies exactly the frequency weighting of mesoscopic fluctuations. The resolvent becomes one test function in a broader Gaussian-field limit rather than an isolated meromorphic observable.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Sine points become a centered counting distribution acting on tests; Fourier covariance defines the Gaussian target; f_z(t)=1/(z-t) later bridges the general theorem back to the logarithmic derivative.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The operator-trace language is explicitly informal because the raw resolvent sum is conditional. The theorem here states finite-dimensional convergence, not yet convergence as a holomorphic random function.
directed.uncertainty: Sobolev and Fourier normalizations are display-dependent but readable.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Dilation pushes every non-Gaussian cumulant and variance-error contribution into a high-frequency region where the test's Fourier mass vanishes, leaving only the H^{1/2} covariance of blue noise.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: CUE cumulant bounds are transferred to the sine process through the virtual-isometry limit. For smooth compact tests, the variance differs from the |k|-weighted Fourier norm only on high frequencies, while cumulants of order at least three are supported where the sum of frequency magnitudes exceeds a fixed cutoff. These bounds extend centered statistics continuously from L1∩H^{1/2} to H^{1/2}. Under f(t/L), the cutoff moves to order L, so variance errors and higher cumulants vanish; density then extends Gaussian convergence to all H^{1/2} tests.
directed.conceptual_reading: Gaussianity emerges by spectral separation: dilation preserves the quadratic low-frequency energy but sends every obstruction to the Fourier tail. The Sobolev extension ensures this mechanism is stable under approximation.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Periodic CUE statistics provide finite-dimensional cumulant formulas; Riemann-sum limits pass them to the sine process; Fourier dilation turns fixed support restrictions into moving high-frequency cutoffs.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The cumulant calculation begins with smooth compact tests and needs a separate L2-continuity/density argument for general H^{1/2}. The conclusion is finite-dimensional in the test index, not automatic process tightness in z.
directed.uncertainty: Hyperplane cumulant integrals are extraction-sensitive; the cutoff, density, and vanishing-cumulant architecture is explicit.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Choosing the resolvent test f_z(t)=1/(z-t) turns the abstract blue-noise limit into a holomorphic Gaussian field; covariance controls both Morera-type holomorphy and the increment bounds needed for compact-open tightness.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The resolvent test lies in H^{1/2} because its Fourier transform is one-sided and exponentially decaying. Smooth cutoffs and H^{1/2} convergence identify its centered statistic with xi_infinity'/xi_infinity minus a half-plane constant. The blue-noise theorem gives finite-dimensional convergence of L times this centered resolvent at Lz to a Gaussian field with explicit half-plane-dependent covariance. A continuous version is shown holomorphic by proving contour integrals vanish in L2, and uniform increment estimates for both prelimit and limit fields give tightness and compact-uniform convergence in law.
directed.conceptual_reading: A single family of test functions converts distribution-valued blue noise into an analytic random function. Holomorphy is not assumed from pointwise Gaussian limits; it is recovered from covariance and contour structure, then paired with tightness.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Fourier transforms place resolvents in H^{1/2}; Proposition 6.4 bridges centered linear statistics to the logarithmic derivative; covariance kernels bridge finite-dimensional convergence to analytic sample paths and process convergence.
directed.boundary_or_failure: All statements live off the real axis; boundary values at the sine points are excluded. Finite-dimensional convergence alone is insufficient, so the separate tightness argument is essential.
directed.uncertainty: Fourier signs, half-plane indicators, and covariance formulas are display-dependent; the cutoff, holomorphy, and tightness arguments are prose-recoverable.
